data.ruling: The datasheet verifier's refutation on "safe operating area during turn-off" stands. The requirement asks for each device to stay inside its single-pulse SOA (safe operating area) while the array opens 300 A (V48) at 17.8 A/us, which takes 16.9 us. It also asks for current sharing across the array (R3 row, Research.md@e13f5f6:281). The pass rests on 300 A dividing equally, 37.5 A a device over 8. During a controlled turn-off every device runs in its saturation region. The datasheet shows that the current there does not divide equally and does not balance itself: (1) Table 4 allows VGS(th) from 2.2 V to 3.8 V, a spread of 1.6 V. (2) Diagram 10: VGS(th) falls as Tj rises. (3) Diagram 7: the 175 degC transfer curve lies above the 25 degC curve below about 5.4 V (about 480 A). At 37.5 A a device the gate sits near 4.2 V to 4.4 V (plateau 4.4 V at 100 A, Table 6). So at a fixed VGS the hotter device carries more current. On the 25 degC transfer curve, a 0.8 V threshold offset between a device at 2.2 V and a typical one at 3.0 V is enough for one device to carry nearly all 300 A while the others carry close to 0 A. Diagram 9's rising RDS(on) covers only the fully-on state at VGS 10 V. One device's allowance over 17 us is 109 A at 85 V (TC 25 degC) and 55 A at TC 100 degC. At 30 V it is 437 A at TC 25 degC and 218 A at TC 100 degC. Every one of these is below 300 A except the 30 V, TC 25 degC case. V49 takes TJ 100 degC at 150 A, so a hot array is the working case. The VDS during turn-off depends on the ESC input capacitance, which is only bounded at 4700 uF at most (V42), so 85 V is the bound. The record itself says the pass holds only with a round-2 gate network, and a gate network in round 2 does not cancel a spread in VGS(th). The scope is the function: the finding is about this function's 300 A turn-off and the division across its placements. It is not about the part's lifecycle, maker or LCSC identity. The stock verifier confirmed stock, lifecycle and identity. The part stays selected for "pack reverse-polarity protection" in selection.json.
data.evidence: The datasheet was fetched again: IPT015N10N5 Rev. 2.4, 2023-05-04, HTTP 200, 970977 bytes. Diagram 3 (ID=f(VDS), TC 25 degC, D=0, single pulse) was rendered at 600 dpi and traced on its gridlines (decade 450.5 px on the x axis, 401.3 px on the y axis). At 30 V the 10 us line is at 666 A and the 100 us line at 106 A. At 85 V the 10 us line is at 206 A and the 100 us line at 13.1 A. Log interpolation at 17 us gives 437 A at 30 V and 109 A at 85 V, and half of that at TC 100 degC gives 218 A and 55 A. These agree with the verifier's 668/107/210/13.4 A and 438/112 A. Table 4: VGS(th) 2.2 V min, 3.0 V typ, 3.8 V max (VDS=VGS, ID 280 uA); gfs 140 S min, 280 S typ. Table 6: Vplateau 4.4 V typ at ID 100 A. Diagram 7: the 175 degC and 25 degC transfer curves cross at about VGS 5.4 V, ID about 480 A, and below that point the 175 degC curve carries more current. Diagram 10: VGS(th) falls from about 3.3 V at 0 degC to about 2.4 V at 100 degC (280 uA curve). Diagram 13: IAV plateau 150 A a device at every Tj(start), so a hard turn-off of 300 A needs avalanche that one device is not rated for, as the record states. Diagram 9: the maximum curve runs 1.50 mOhm at 25 degC to 2.19 mOhm at 100 degC, at VGS 10 V and ID 150 A only. No figure in the datasheet states how current divides between parallel devices in the saturation region. P2 record (scratch FU-A3/P2-R3/return.json, rank 1): "37.5 A a device over 8 is inside at 85 V (56 A); at 30 V one device could carry 220 A. Holds only with the gate network that sets the rate (round 2)".
